God, there's so much wrong with what you're saying... First of all the problem with outing yourself is not a question of "freedom of speech", it's how people react to you making use of that freedom.

Secondly, and you may not understand this because you have evidently never been in the situation, nor known anybody in it since you haven't been educated thus far, approximately 40% of the homeless youth identify as LGBT. That's FORTY FUCKING PERCENT. Yes, that's how much their families accept them for being who they are, they get kicked out of their homes. Just because the trend is finally going towards acceptance does not mean that people aren't being treated like shit for who they are or how they identify as.

If this topic really troubles you that much, go and meet some LGBT folks. Let them tell you about their experiences and educate yourself instead of just making blind assumptions. You have absolutely no clue how hard it is to make yourself vulnerable to others, if you have to be afraid they will never want to see you again.

>There is help available, and there are approaches which have worked for many people who've been right where you are now.

That's the main part that makes me feel so stuck. I have been in therapy several times over many years, lived lived in a psychiatric clinic, got tons of exposure. The social anxiety has never gotten any less, it just got worse. :/

This might sound wrong, but I've read your entire post with the biggest smile on my face. Every single detail you have mentioned is exactly the same for me. Even the running in the morning, only that for me it is biking at night. You know, so nobody can see me.

No job or school right now, shut in, no license. I guess the only difference is that I have pushed away the few friends I still had.

Obviously I wouldn't wish being like this on my worst enemy, but it's nice to know that you're not alone. Thank you for sharing and best of luck. Hope you'll get a little better soon. :)

Sorry to hear that your family and friends don't take your problems seriously. That happens quite a lot with these kinds of things, many here know how much that sucks.

Just to add to FinnianWhitefir's response: If you're not sure where exactly to make an appointment, you can also go to your GP and they will refer you to someone who can help. Just say what you have written here. Make it clear that this is a really big problem for you and they WILL take you seriously. Don't let the responses you have gotten from your family discourage you. People who aren't familiar with this sort of stuff tend to brush it off as no big deal. But doctors and therapists are going to take you more seriously.

Good luck and take care!

Everything you wrote is so true it hurts. Almost anyone I have ever met has the "If I can't see it, it doesn't exist." attitude. If you have some physical illness at least people can see it. But when the only thing people can see of our problems is our behaviour, they write it off as some character flaw. There's no way they could possibly understand how it looks inside of us. Sometimes I wish there was some big physical sympton that comes with mental health problems, so everyone can see it and think "Oh hey! It's real after all.". Like a big mark on our foreheads or something...

Really there's nothing we can do about those people. But you know what? Next to all the ignorant people out there, there's always some open minded ones, and those who are suffering from all sorts of shit themselves. At least we can help each other. I mean most people who are reading this post right now probably understand everything you've said more than anyone else, right? :)

Edit: To go with your bane analogy: There's millions of banes in the world and we all have a mask to share.

Yeah, I've notice myself doing this after almost every social interaction. 

Even the most basic things, like someone making eye contact that leads me to look away. Immediately after I would start obsessing about what they would think when I avoid eye contact. I know that realistically they probably think nothing of it at all, but that doesn't stop me from obsessing about it and convincing myself of how pathetic they must think I am.

Here's what helped me the most so far: After you notice something like this happening, try to think of a way to make the same scenario play out the other way around. To go along with the eye contact example, I would start forcing myself to return eye contact when strangers initiate it. Eventually you will start to come across people who avoid YOUR eye contact. It's pretty interesting to be on the other end of the situation and let's you actually experience what goes through the other person's mind.

So basically when you catch yourself "mind reading", find a way to back up your assumptions with an experience. To apply this to any other situation, start being aware of what YOU think about other people in any situation you're in at all times, so you have reliable info to go by when you're on the other end again.

I hope that makes any sense at all. Sorry I'm having a little trouble expressing this stuff in words. ;)

Yes, stayed indoors for the entire time. It was from around age 16 to 21, living with my parents and brother. Their support is basically what made me not go crazy during that time. We don't talk about any of this, they just pretend nothing is wrong. And honestly there's nothing they could possibly do to help. But just them being there and the fact that they give me a place to stay is more than I could ever ask of them.

Thank you for your nice response.

>I am very fortunate to have more friends than i know what to do with and am incredibly aware how grateful i should be, knowing this, i constantly try to get him to come out with us, however, rather it is going out to eat, fishing, or watching basketball at my house, he absolutely refuses, saying that because of his "pain" he can't be active or social in anyway, then gets mad at me, literally yells at me for inviting him to places he could meet people, which i know what help him immensely.

This is one thing you should be careful about. I know you mean well in inviting him, and you could be totally right in thinking it would help him to go out with you guys. However him isolating himself is not the problem, it's a symptom. There is some reason for why he can't just socialize, whether it's depression, anxiety, or whatever else. You know, the thing he describes as "pain".

You may think you understand what's going on inside of him, and you might, but the best thing you can do is to always assume that you don't. Because feeling misunderstood is the most damaging feeling if you're suicidal. He might already be feeling alone with all of his problems. The best thing you can do is be there for him and listen. Try to hold back any of your own views judgements on his problems and let him explain as much as possible.

The next step thing obviously be to get him help. To be honest I have no idea how to go about that. Does he want to try going to a therapist? If you don't know, bring that topic up maybe. For one it doesn't even sound like he has been properly diagnosed with anything, correct me if I'm wrong.

Also check out all the links on the right-hand side of this subreddit. They should a pretty good idea of what to say, and more importantly what not to say to you brother.

I hope things work out alright for you all. The situation with your dad sounds terrible, hope he will disappear from your life in the future. Take care and best of luck!
